### Problem: Replace Non-Coprime Numbers in Array {#sec-gcd-p5-merge}

::: {.p-statement}
**Collapse every non-coprime run into its LCM.** Repeatedly find two *adjacent* elements
whose gcd exceeds $1$; replace that pair with a single element equal to their least common
multiple. Keep going until no adjacent pair shares a factor, and return the resulting array.
The test cases guarantee the final array is unique regardless of the order you merge.

```text
[6, 4, 3, 2, 7, 6, 2]  -> [12, 7, 6]
[2, 2, 1, 1, 3, 3, 3]  -> [2, 1, 1, 3]
```

For `[6, 4, 3, 2, 7, 6, 2]` the leading run $6,4,3,2$ is chained by shared factors
($\gcd(6,4)=2$, $\gcd(12,3)=3$, $\gcd(12,2)=2$) so it folds to $\mathrm{lcm}=12$; the $7$
is coprime to everything beside it; the tail $6,2$ folds to $6$. Result: `[12, 7, 6]`.

**Constraints.** $1 \le n \le 10^5$; $1 \le \mathit{nums}[i] \le 10^6$.
Source: [LC 2197 · Replace Non-Coprime Numbers in Array](https://leetcode.com/problems/replace-non-coprime-numbers-in-array/){.solved difficulty="Hard"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
Merging is *associative along a run*: if $a,b$ share a factor and $b,c$ share a factor, the
whole stretch $a,b,c$ ends up as $\mathrm{lcm}(a,b,c)$ no matter how you bracket it, because
$\mathrm{lcm}$ absorbs prime powers monotonically. So the answer is just "maximal runs of
pairwise-connected elements, each replaced by its LCM". A left-to-right **stack** finds those
runs in one pass: push each number, and while the top shares a factor with the incoming
number, pop and fold the LCM back - the running LCM keeps growing so it will absorb the whole
run. This is the pigeonhole view of @sec-gcd-a6: an element can only be absorbed a bounded
number of times (its prime-power content is capped), so the stack work is near-linear.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Merge any adjacent pair, repeatedly.** Scan left to right, fold the first non-coprime
   adjacent pair into its LCM, restart until no pair qualifies. The definition; $O(n^2)$ or
   worse with the restarts.
2. **One left-to-right stack.** Push each element; while $\gcd(\text{top}, x) > 1$ pop and
   set $x = \mathrm{lcm}(\text{top}, x)$; push the folded $x$. Each element is pushed and
   popped once, so $O(n \log V)$ with a $\gcd$ costing $O(\log V)$.
:::

::: {#fig-gcd-p5-merge}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    V.grid(ax, p, [["run", "[6,4,3,2]", "[7]", "[6,2]"],
                   ["lcm", "12", "7", "6"]],
           colors={(1, 1): "cyan", (1, 3): "cyan"}, cell_w=1.6)
V.show(draw)
```

The input splits into maximal merge-runs. The first run folds to $12$ and the last to $6$
(cyan); the lone $7$ is already a fixed point. Reading off the run LCMs gives `[12, 7, 6]`.

:::

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Merge the first adjacent pair, over and over

::: {.form-next}
The literal rule: repeatedly scan for the leftmost adjacent pair with $\gcd > 1$ and replace
it with the pair's LCM, shrinking the array by one, until a full sweep finds no mergeable
pair. Correct by definition and easy to trust, but the rescans make it $O(n^2)$.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("merge", "naive")
    assert str(final) == "[12, 7, 6]"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def mr_naive(nums):
    a = list(nums)
    changed = True
    while changed:
        changed = False
        for i in range(len(a) - 1):
            if math.gcd(a[i], a[i + 1]) > 1:
                a[i:i + 2] = [a[i] // math.gcd(a[i], a[i + 1]) * a[i + 1]]
                changed = True
                break
    return a

assert mr_naive([6, 4, 3, 2, 7, 6, 2]) == [12, 7, 6]
assert mr_naive([2, 2, 1, 1, 3, 3, 3]) == [2, 1, 1, 3]
```

##### C++

```cpp
long long mygcd(long long a, long long b) {
    while (b) { long long t = a % b; a = b; b = t; }
    return a;
}

vector<long long> mrNaive(vector<long long>& nums) {
    vector<long long> a = nums;
    bool changed = true;
    while (changed) {
        changed = false;
        for (int i = 0; i + 1 < (int) a.size(); ++i) {
            long long g = mygcd(a[i], a[i + 1]);
            if (g > 1) { a[i] = a[i] / g * a[i + 1]; a.erase(a.begin() + i + 1); changed = true; break; }
        }
    }
    return a;
}
```

:::

#### Fold runs with one stack

::: {.form-next}
Walk left to right keeping a stack of already-finalised run LCMs. For each new $x$, keep
popping the top while $\gcd(\text{top}, x) > 1$ and folding $x = \mathrm{lcm}(\text{top}, x)$;
then push $x$. Because a fold only grows $x$'s prime powers, one pass captures every maximal
run. $O(n \log V)$.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("merge", "stack")
    assert str(final) == "[12, 7, 6]"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def mr_stack(nums):
    st = []
    for x in nums:
        cur = x
        while st and math.gcd(st[-1], cur) > 1:
            top = st.pop()
            cur = top // math.gcd(top, cur) * cur
        st.append(cur)
    return st

assert mr_stack([6, 4, 3, 2, 7, 6, 2]) == [12, 7, 6]
assert mr_stack([2, 2, 1, 1, 3, 3, 3]) == [2, 1, 1, 3]
for _ in range(300):
    a = [random.randint(1, 20) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 10))]
    assert mr_stack(a) == mr_naive(a), a
```

##### C++

```cpp
long long mygcd(long long a, long long b) {
    while (b) { long long t = a % b; a = b; b = t; }
    return a;
}

vector<long long> mrStack(vector<long long>& nums) {
    vector<long long> st;
    for (long long x : nums) {
        long long cur = x;
        while (!st.empty() && mygcd(st.back(), cur) > 1) {
            long long g = mygcd(st.back(), cur);
            cur = st.back() / g * cur;
            st.pop_back();
        }
        st.push_back(cur);
    }
    return st;
}
```

:::

:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Time.** Rung 1 is $O(n^2 \log V)$ with its restarts; rung 2 is $O(n \log V)$ - each element
pushed and popped at most once, every $\gcd$/$\mathrm{lcm}$ costing $O(\log V)$. **Space.**
$O(n)$ for the stack. Compute $\mathrm{lcm}$ as $a / \gcd \cdot b$, not $a \cdot b / \gcd$,
and keep it in 64-bit to avoid overflow.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- **All coprime.** `[2, 1, 1, 3]`-style inputs never merge: every adjacent $\gcd$ is $1$, so
  the stack just echoes the array (modulo the $1$-runs, which also stay put).
- **Everything merges.** `[2, 2, 2, 2]` collapses to the single value $2$; the stack pops and
  re-folds each time, ending at one element.
- **Ones are blockers.** $\gcd(1, x) = 1$ for all $x$, so a $1$ never merges - it terminates a
  run, which is why `[2,2,1,1,3,3,3]` keeps the middle `1, 1` in the output.

**Debug tip.** If your result merges a $1$ with a neighbour, you used `>= 1` instead of `> 1`
for the gcd test - $\gcd$ is always at least $1$, so the real condition to merge is $\gcd > 1$.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistakes"}
- Deciding adjacency *transitively*: after folding $6,4 \to 12$, the $12$ becomes adjacent to
  $3$ and can absorb it - you must re-test the *new* top against the incoming value, which is
  exactly what the `while` loop does.
- Overflowing the LCM by writing `a * b / gcd`. Divide first: `a / gcd * b`, in `long long`.
- Forgetting that the fold is monotone: once absorbed, a run's LCM never shrinks, so a single
  left-to-right pass is enough - no second sweep backward is needed.
:::

**Variants.** @sec-gcd-p5-parity is the other "large input forces the answer" problem - there
a pigeonhole count replaces any simulation entirely; @sec-gcd-p2-rects also reduces a stream
to canonical keys but tallies them instead of merging neighbours; @sec-gcd-a6 supplies the
bounded-absorption argument that keeps the stack linear.
